name: European oak (Quercus robur and Q. petraea)
summary: The museum's one timber: the heartwood of European oak, a ring-porous hardwood with broad rays and a high tannin content, sawn quarter or plain, fumed or left natural, and finished in a hardwax oil or wax. It is the Salon's Versailles parquet and the plinths of its velvet benches, the 1874 case, the Reserve's picture screens, chests and easel, the oval's pond-bench seats, and Albion's cases, lectern and benches.

formation.how: Oak lays down one ring a year under the bark. Each ring opens with a band of large earlywood vessels (ring-porous) and closes with dense latewood fibre; broad rays run radially from pith to bark. As the tree ages the inner sapwood dies and becomes heartwood: its vessels are plugged by tyloses and its cells fill with extractives, chiefly tannins, which colour it brown, make it durable, react with ammonia (fuming) and stain blue-black with iron when wet. The nearly white sapwood is cut away.

unfinishedSurfaceScatter.text: Planing and sanding leave a layer of broken cells whose irregular surface scatters white light diffusely, which is why unfinished wood looks light and unsaturated; a clear finish whose index is close to the cell wall's removes that first interface, so colour deepens and the subsurface highlight appears.

fibreHighlight.text: Finished wood shows a subsurface highlight that no surface-anisotropy model reproduces: light enters, scatters from the aligned fibres below the surface and leaves on a cone about the local fibre axis, which can tilt out of the surface plane. The model adds a fibre term (fibre axis u, fibre colour k_f, and a Gaussian highlight width beta, one per species) to a Fresnel-corrected diffuse term and the finish's own surface specular; both subsurface terms are attenuated by Fresnel transmission in and out through the finish. On interlocked grain the highlight swings 30-40 degrees either side of the normal across the figure. Measured samples: varnished walnut, lacquered walnut, lacquered curly maple, varnished padauk; oak was not measured.

acidEmission.text: Wood and wood products, unless sealed, emit organic acids; oak and cedar are the problem woods. An enclosure built of poorly chosen wood and paint causes problems, and lead is the material most sensitive to acetic acid. Sealing the wood (acrylic latex paint with at least four weeks' drying) and basic control of RH mitigate it; low-permeability interleaves (buffered paper, PET film) separate objects from the source.

photograph: Coarse, open texture: the earlywood pores read as fine dark dashes in bands along the grain, filled grey-brown where old wax and dirt sit in them.
On quarter-sawn faces, silvery ray flecks crossing the straight stripe, which flash light or dark as the view turns.
On plain-sawn faces, arched 'cathedral' figure and a tone that changes board to board; no two boards alike.
Under oil or wax, a warm colour with depth and a soft band of sheen that moves across the grain as you walk, not a uniform plastic gloss.
Fumed oak: a cool, even, grey-brown to chocolate brown, the rays paler than the ground; a lighter tone where a worn edge cuts through a surface-fumed layer.
On a parquet, paths of duller, paler finish where people walk, and fine gaps at panel edges in winter.

unverified.reason: Converting the SATRA PTVs with the UK Slip Resistance Group relation mu = 3 PTV / (330 - PTV) gives about 0.65 dry and 0.36 wet; the relation was not read at its source.
EN 13226 is widely quoted as requiring solid parquet delivered at 7-11 % moisture content; the standard was not read.
Broad-ray widths of about 0.15-1.04 mm are reported for Quercus species in a search summary; no oak anatomy source was read.

unverified.reason: No measured L*a*b* of European oak under a hardwax oil or wax was read; a finish darkens and saturates bare wood (Marschner et al. 2005), by an amount to be measured on a tier (b) specimen.
Marschner et al. fitted one highlight width per species but did not measure oak and do not print the values.
